course.title: Logic and Reasoning
course.description: Work out what follows from what. Read arguments carefully, test them against cases, and see where everyday reasoning goes wrong.
course.audience: A general reader with no background in formal logic who wants to argue and evaluate arguments more carefully.

modules.title: Deduction
modules.description: What it means for a conclusion to follow from its premises, and how to test whether it does.

modules.title: Arguments
modules.description: Telling a good argument from a persuasive one, and naming the ways reasoning fails.

concepts.title: Statement
concepts.summary: A sentence that is either true or false, which is what logic operates on.

concepts.title: Conditional
concepts.summary: An if-then claim, which is false only when the antecedent holds and the consequent fails.

concepts.title: Truth table
concepts.summary: An exhaustive listing of the cases a compound statement can take.

concepts.title: Negation and converse
concepts.summary: Turning a conditional around or inside out changes what it claims.

concepts.title: Premise and conclusion
concepts.summary: The claims offered as support, and the claim they are meant to support.

concepts.title: Validity and soundness
concepts.summary: Whether the conclusion follows, and separately whether the premises are true.

concepts.title: Fallacy
concepts.summary: A pattern of reasoning that persuades without supporting.

lessons.title: What logic operates on

blocks.text: A claim has a truth value

Let p stand for “The lamp is on.” Toggle p between true and false. We can ask which value this claim has even when we cannot see the lamp. A question asks for information; a command asks someone to act.
Unknown does not mean neither

Let p mean “The sealed box contains a coin.” The box already has some contents, although you do not know them. In this course, each claim has one truth value in a case. Your uncertainty about p does not create a third value.
Negation reverses the value

The symbol ¬p means “not p”. Select each value of p and read the result. If the lamp is on, “the lamp is not on” is false. Negation changes the claim being made; it does not report your confidence in that claim.
Disagreement still concerns a claim

Let p mean “This painting is beautiful.” People may dispute its truth or use different standards. That does not turn it into a question or a command. Logical form alone does not settle aesthetic truth. Distinguish the kind of sentence from evidence for it.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish truth-apt claims from questions and commands, including claims whose truth is unknown or disputed.
lessons.nextAction: A claim can be true or false, even when its truth is unknown.

lessons.title: If-then claims

blocks.text: Find the broken rule

Let p mean “The access code is correct” and q mean “The door opens.” The rule p → q says that a correct code is sufficient for an open door. Toggle the two claims to find the case where the rule fails.
Only one row fails

The material conditional is false exactly when its antecedent p is true and its consequent q is false. The other three rows make it true. This definition describes truth values; it does not establish that entering a code physically causes a door to open.
A false starting condition

Set p false and q false. The conditional is true because this case does not break its rule. You cannot infer q from the conditional alone. There might be another way to open the door, or it might remain closed.
Try another subject

Let p mean “A shape is a square” and q mean “It has four sides.” A four-sided rectangle can make p false and q true. That case respects the conditional while showing why observing q alone does not establish p.

lessons.orientation: State exactly when a conditional is false, and resist the pull to read it as a promise about the antecedent.
lessons.nextAction: Recognise that a conditional and its contrapositive say the same thing, while its converse does not.

lessons.title: Converse and contrapositive

blocks.text: Reversing the arrow

Compare p → q with q → p. The second is the converse: it exchanges the antecedent and consequent. Set p false and q true in both tables. One rule permits this case and the other rejects it, so they are not equivalent.
Reverse and negate

The contrapositive of p → q is ¬q → ¬p. Its only false case is q false and p true, exactly the original rule’s false case. Toggle all four assignments. Matching every row establishes equivalence for these truth-functional formulas.
Repair the flipped inference

If a file is encrypted, it needs a key. Knowing that it needs a key does not establish that it is encrypted: other access rules could also require a key. A counterexample keeps the original conditional true while making the proposed conclusion false.
Carry the rule to a new case

If a parcel is fragile, it gets a warning label. The contrapositive says that a parcel without a warning label is not fragile, assuming the rule holds. The converse would say every labelled parcel is fragile, which the rule does not guarantee.

lessons.orientation: Recognise that a conditional and its contrapositive say the same thing, while its converse does not.
lessons.nextAction: Solve a small puzzle by assuming a case and following it to a contradiction.

lessons.title: Knights and knaves

blocks.text: Assume a speaker’s type

A knight always tells the truth; a knave always lies. Ada says “Ben is a knave.” Let p mean Ada is a knight and q mean Ben is a knight. Ada’s claim has value ¬q. Consistency requires p and ¬q to have the same value.
Keep both consistent cases

If Ada is a knave, her claim that Ben is a knave is false, making Ben a knight. That leaves two assignments: Ada knight with Ben knave, or Ada knave with Ben knight. The statement alone does not tell us which assignment holds.
Add a second statement

Ben now says “Ada and I are the same type.” In either surviving assignment their types differ, so Ben’s claim is false. Ben must therefore be a knave. That rules out the case in which Ben was a knight and leaves Ada as a knight.
Change the speaker’s claim

Cara says “Drew is a knight.” Drew says “Cara is a knave.” If Cara were a knight, Drew would also be a knight, contradicting Drew’s statement. If Cara is a knave, Drew is a knave, yet Drew’s statement becomes true. Both cases fail.

lessons.orientation: Solve a small puzzle by assuming a case and following it to a contradiction.
lessons.nextAction: Enumerate the cases of a two-variable compound statement and read validity off the result.

lessons.title: Building a truth table

blocks.text: List every assignment

For two claims p and q, each can independently be true or false. The table lists TT, TF, FT and FF. Selecting a row helps you inspect one case without losing the others. An exhaustive table must include every assignment exactly once.
Conjunction needs both

The conjunction p ∧ q is true only when both claims are true. Inclusive disjunction p ∨ q needs at least one true claim, so it also permits both. Change the selected row and compare its two inputs with the result.
Inclusive or allows overlap

Here p ∨ q is true in TT, TF and FT. Everyday “or” sometimes excludes overlap, but the symbol ∨ in this course is inclusive. The definition settles that ambiguity before we use the table to check an argument.
A counterexample is enough

Consider “p ∨ q; p; therefore ¬q”. Its premises are true when p and q are both true, but its conclusion is false. Select that row. One counterexample is enough to refute validity; the other rows cannot cancel it.

lessons.orientation: Enumerate the cases of a two-variable compound statement and read validity off the result.
lessons.nextAction: Separate an argument's conclusion from the claims offered in its support.

lessons.title: Finding the conclusion

blocks.text: Support points toward a conclusion

If the battery is charged, the torch lights. The battery is charged. Therefore the torch lights. Let p name the battery claim and q the lighting claim. The first two sentences are premises; the last is the conclusion they support.
Filter for true premises

To test “p → q; p; therefore q”, inspect assignments where both premises are true. The conditional rules out TF, and the second premise rules out rows with p false. Only TT survives. The conclusion q is true there.
The conclusion can come first

“The torch lights, because the battery is charged and a charged battery makes it light” puts the conclusion first. Position alone does not determine a sentence’s role. Ask what the speaker wants you to accept and which claims are offered as support.
Follow a different pattern

Either the parcel is at the desk or it is in the locker. It is not at the desk. Therefore it is in the locker. Let p be the desk claim and q the locker claim. Inspect p false while the disjunction remains true.

lessons.orientation: Separate an argument's conclusion from the claims offered in its support.
lessons.nextAction: Judge whether a conclusion follows separately from whether the premises are true.

lessons.title: Valid but untrue

blocks.text: Form can survive false premises

Suppose “If every stone floats, this stone floats” and “Every stone floats.” The conclusion “This stone floats” follows from those premises by the pattern p → q; p; therefore q. The false premise does not break that inference pattern.
Validity excludes a counterexample

An argument is valid when there is no case with all premises true and the conclusion false. It can still contain false premises or have a false conclusion in the actual world. Soundness adds the requirement that every premise is actually true.
A true ending is not enough

Consider “p → q; q; therefore p”. Set p false and q true. Both premises hold but the conclusion fails. The argument remains invalid even if a different actual case happens to make its conclusion true. Test the guarantee, rather than one happy outcome.
Judge two properties separately

A valid argument whose premises are all true is sound. A valid argument with a false premise is unsound. Truth of the conclusion alone settles neither property. First test the inference across cases, then investigate the premises with suitable evidence.

lessons.orientation: Judge whether a conclusion follows separately from whether the premises are true.
lessons.nextAction: Identify affirming the consequent, denying the antecedent, and attacking the person.

lessons.title: Naming the fallacies

blocks.text: An effect can have another cause

If a sensor overheats, its warning light turns on. The light is on, so the sensor overheated. This affirms the consequent. The light could have another cause. Set p false and q true to keep both premises true while refuting the conclusion.
Removing a cause does not remove every effect

If the sensor overheats, the light turns on. It did not overheat, so the light is off. This denies the antecedent. Another trigger could still turn the light on. The same false–true assignment exposes the missing guarantee in this argument.
Repair the inference

With p → q and ¬q, the conclusion ¬p does follow: a true p would require q, contradicting ¬q. This pattern is called modus tollens. Toggle the assignments and keep only those where the conditional and ¬q are both true.
A label needs a reason

“Their calculation must be wrong because they are rude” attacks the person without checking the calculation. A useful criticism identifies a faulty step or missing premise. Calling an argument a fallacy is incomplete unless you explain the gap in support.

lessons.orientation: Identify affirming the consequent, denying the antecedent, and attacking the person.
lessons.nextAction: Try the changed cases in your review queue.

questions.prompt: Which sentence makes a claim?
hints: A claim asserts something that could be true or false.
Compare an assertion with a question or an instruction.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ‘The lamp is on’ asserts a condition that can be true or false. A question requests information, and a command directs an action.

questions.prompt: How many truth values do we use for a claim in classical logic?
hints: This course uses classical two-valued logic.
List its possible truth values, then count them.
Whether we know the truth is separate from how many truth values the model uses.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A claim is true or false in a case: two values.

questions.prompt: When p is true, is ¬p true or false?
hints: The symbol ¬ means negation.
Negation switches the truth value of the original claim.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Negation reverses true to false.

questions.prompt: How should we treat “This painting is beautiful” here?
hints: The speaker is asserting an evaluation, even though people may disagree.
Disagreement does not turn an assertion into a question or a command.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The sentence asserts an evaluation, so it is treated here as a disputed claim. Disagreement about beauty does not make the sentence a command.

questions.prompt: Is “Close the window” a claim or a command? Use one word.
hints: Ask whether the sentence states a fact or directs someone to act.
The verb 'Close' is asking for an action.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It directs an action, rather than asserting a truth.

questions.prompt: A claim is false. Is its negation true or false?
hints: Apply negation to the stated false truth value.
The negated claim has the opposite value.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The negation of a false claim is true.

questions.prompt: Which case makes p → q false?
hints: An if-then claim rules out the antecedent holding while the consequent fails.
Look for the row that breaks that guarantee.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The material conditional p → q fails when p is true and q is false: its antecedent holds, but the promised consequent does not.

questions.prompt: How many of the four rows make p → q true?
hints: List TT, TF, FT and FF.
A material conditional fails only when its antecedent is true and consequent false.
Count the remaining rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the true–false row is false, so three rows are true.

questions.prompt: When p and q are both false, is p → q true or false?
hints: The antecedent p is false in this case.
A false antecedent does not violate the material conditional's guarantee.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A false antecedent makes the material conditional true.

questions.prompt: Let p mean “The shape is a square” and q mean “The shape has four sides.” For a non-square rectangle with four sides, is p true or false?
hints: Here p is the statement that the shape is a square.
A four-sided shape need not satisfy that more specific description.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The rectangle has four sides but is not a square, so p is false.

questions.prompt: p is true and q is false. Is p → q true or false?
hints: Check the row in which the antecedent holds but the consequent does not.
That row is the one excluded by the implication.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its antecedent holds and its consequent fails.

questions.prompt: How many rows make a two-claim material conditional false?
hints: Inspect each possible assignment to p and q.
A counterexample requires p to hold and q to fail.
Count the assignments meeting both conditions.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There is exactly one false row: true antecedent, false consequent.

questions.prompt: Is q → p true or false when q is true and p is false?
hints: In q → p, q is the antecedent and p is the consequent.
Apply the same implication rule after the order has changed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The converse has a true antecedent and a false consequent.

questions.prompt: Across four assignments, how many rows differ between p → q and ¬q → ¬p?
hints: Compare each row of p → q with the matching row of ¬q → ¬p.
Negate both inputs and reverse their order for the second expression.
Count disagreements, not true rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Their truth values match in every row, so none differ.

questions.prompt: Which case defeats “p → q; q; therefore p”?
hints: A counterexample must keep both premises true and make the conclusion false.
Set the conclusion p to false, then choose q so that both premises still hold.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With p false and q true, both p → q and q are true, while the conclusion p is false. That single case refutes the inference.

questions.prompt: Choose the contrapositive of “If fragile, then labelled”.
hints: A contrapositive reverses the two claims and negates both.
The original consequent 'labelled' becomes the negated antecedent.

acceptedIdeas: If not labelled, then not fragile
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Reverse the original claims and negate both: ‘If not labelled, then not fragile.’ This contrapositive has the same truth values as the original conditional.

choices.label: If not labelled, then not fragile
If not fragile, then not labelled

questions.prompt: What is q → p called relative to p → q?
hints: This transformation exchanges the original antecedent and consequent.
It does not negate either claim.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Exchanging the two claims gives the converse.

questions.prompt: What is ¬q → ¬p called relative to p → q?
hints: This transformation both reverses the order and negates the claims.
Distinguish it from merely exchanging p and q.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Reversing and negating both claims gives the contrapositive.

questions.prompt: Knights always tell the truth; knaves always lie. Ada says, “Ben is a knave.” If Ada is a knight, must Ben be a knight or a knave?
hints: A knight's statement must be true.
Apply that rule to Ada's exact claim about Ben.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A truthful Ada says Ben is a knave, so Ben is a knave.

questions.prompt: Knights always tell the truth; knaves always lie. Ada says, “Ben is a knave.” How many assignments of their types fit Ada’s statement?
hints: Test Ada as a knight, then as a knave.
In each case choose Ben's type to make Ada's statement consistent with hers.
Keep every consistent assignment; one statement may leave several.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Either Ada is truthful and Ben a knave, or Ada lies and Ben is a knight.

questions.prompt: Knights always tell the truth; knaves always lie. Ada says, “Ben is a knave.” Ben says, “Ada and I are the same type.” Is Ada a knight or a knave?
hints: In both surviving cases Ada and Ben have different types.
Ben's claim that their types match is false; use that to determine his type and then Ada's.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ben lies, so Ben is a knave and Ada’s claim is true.

questions.prompt: Knights always tell the truth; knaves always lie. Cara says, “Drew is a knight.” Drew says, “Cara is a knave.” How many consistent assignments of their types fit both statements?
hints: Try Cara as a knight and check Drew's statement.
Then try Cara as a knave and check whether Drew tells the truth.
Count only assignments in which both speakers obey their own type.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Assuming either type for Cara produces a contradiction, leaving zero assignments.

questions.prompt: Ada is a knave and says “Ben is a knave.” Is Ben a knight or a knave?
hints: A knave's statement is false.
Negate Ada's claim about Ben rather than accepting it.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ada’s claim is false, so Ben is a knight.

questions.prompt: How many assignments should you test for two people with two possible types each?
hints: There are two type choices for Ada and two for Ben.
Pair each first person's choice with every second person's choice.
Multiply the numbers of choices to count all assignments.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two choices for each person give 2 × 2 = 4 assignments.

questions.prompt: How many assignments are needed for p and q?
hints: Each of p and q can be true or false.
Pair each value of p with both possible values of q.
Count all distinct assignments, including the all-false one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two values for p times two for q gives four assignments.

questions.prompt: How many rows make p ∧ q true?
hints: The connective ∧ requires both claims to hold.
Inspect TT, TF, FT and FF.
Count only rows with two true inputs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the TT row makes both claims true.

questions.prompt: How many rows make p ∨ q true?
hints: Inclusive ∨ requires at least one true input.
Do not exclude the row where both inputs are true.
Count the rows other than the all-false row.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At least one claim is true in three of the four rows.

questions.prompt: Consider the argument “p ∨ q; p; therefore ¬q”. Which assignment is a counterexample?
hints: Keep both premises p ∨ q and p true.
To defeat the conclusion ¬q, q must also be true.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: When p and q are both true, the premises p ∨ q and p hold, but the conclusion ¬q is false. Inclusive ‘or’ permits this counterexample.

questions.prompt: Three independent claims each have two truth values. How many rows are needed?
hints: Each additional claim doubles the combinations.
Use two choices for each of three separate claims.
Multiply those three numbers of choices.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The row count is 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.

questions.prompt: Can inclusive p ∨ q be true when both claims are true? Answer yes or no.
hints: The word inclusive matters here.
At least one true claim permits the case with two true claims.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Inclusive disjunction allows both claims to be true.

questions.prompt: “If the battery is charged, the torch lights. The battery is charged. Therefore the torch lights.” In this argument, is “The torch lights” a premise or a conclusion?
hints: Identify the statement the other sentences are offered to support.
The word 'therefore' points toward that role in this passage.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is the conclusion supported by the two premises.

questions.prompt: How many rows make both p → q and p true?
hints: First keep rows with p true.
Of those, discard any row that makes p → q false.
Count rows satisfying both premises at once.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only TT makes both premises true.

questions.prompt: “The torch lights, because the battery is charged and a charged battery makes it light.” In this passage, is “The battery is charged” a premise or a conclusion?
hints: The sentence's role depends on what it supports, not where it appears.
In this passage the charged battery is offered as the reason the torch lights.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It supplies support, so it is a premise.

questions.prompt: “Either the parcel is at the desk or it is in the locker. It is not at the desk. Therefore it is in the locker.” Which location is the conclusion: desk or locker?
hints: The first premise gives two possible locations.
The second premise eliminates the desk location.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The parcel must be in the locker given the two premises.

questions.prompt: What do we call a claim offered as support for a conclusion?
hints: This is the supporting part of an argument.
Distinguish the evidence offered from the claim it is meant to establish.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A premise is offered in support of the conclusion.

questions.prompt: In “p → q; p; therefore q”, which letter is the conclusion?
hints: Look at the statement after 'therefore'.
The two earlier statements are being used to support that letter.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The conclusion is q.

questions.prompt: Is the pattern “p → q; p; therefore q” valid or invalid?
hints: Ask whether both premises can be true while q is false.
The first premise links p to q, and the second states p.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No assignment makes its premises true and its conclusion false.

questions.prompt: How many counterexamples may a valid argument have?
hints: Validity is a guarantee over every possible assignment.
A true-premise, false-conclusion case would break that guarantee.
Count how many such exceptions the definition permits.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A single counterexample would make it invalid, so a valid argument has none.

questions.prompt: Is the argument “p → q; q; therefore p” valid or invalid?
hints: Try p false and q true in the displayed argument.
Check both premises and then compare their values with the conclusion p.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The false–true assignment supplies a counterexample.

questions.prompt: A valid argument contains a false premise. Is it sound or unsound?
hints: Soundness requires two conditions: validity and true premises.
Check whether the stated false premise meets the second condition.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Soundness requires validity and all true premises.

questions.prompt: A valid argument has all true premises. Is it sound or unsound?
hints: Recall both parts of the definition of soundness.
The question supplies validity and truth of every premise.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It meets both requirements for soundness.

questions.prompt: How many true-premise, false-conclusion cases are needed to refute validity?
hints: Validity says there are no cases of true premises with a false conclusion.
One exception is enough to break a universal guarantee.
You do not need a majority of the truth table to be counterexamples.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One counterexample disproves the guarantee.

questions.prompt: Which assignment refutes “p → q; q; therefore p”?
hints: Keep p → q true and keep q true.
To refute the conclusion p, choose its false value.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The assignment p false, q true keeps both premises true and makes the conclusion false. A true consequent does not establish its antecedent.

questions.prompt: In the counterexample p false and q true, is the conclusion ¬q true or false?
hints: The conclusion is ¬q, not q.
Apply negation to the stated value q = true.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The conclusion ¬q is false because q is true.

questions.prompt: For “p → q; ¬q; therefore ¬p”, is the pattern valid or invalid?
hints: Suppose p were true while q is false.
Would that satisfy the first premise p → q?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both premises force p false, so ¬p follows.

questions.prompt: Someone argues, “Their calculation must be wrong because they are rude.” Which response examines the reasoning?
hints: A criticism of someone's manners does not check their calculation.
Choose a response that examines the claimed step or supporting evidence.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Checking the disputed calculation step addresses the reasoning. The person's manners alone do not establish whether the calculation is correct.

choices.label: Treat the speaker’s popularity as proof

questions.prompt: In “p → q; q; therefore p”, which named part is affirmed: antecedent or consequent?
hints: In p → q, p comes before the arrow and q after it.
The extra premise asserts q; name that part of the conditional.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: q is the consequent, which the argument affirms.

questions.prompt: In “p → q; ¬p; therefore ¬q”, which part is denied: antecedent or consequent?
hints: Identify the part represented by p in p → q.
The extra premise ¬p denies that part.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: p is the antecedent, which the argument denies.

flashcards.front: When p is false, what truth value does ¬p have?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The negation is true.

flashcards.front: What kind of sentence is “Where is the key?”: claim, question or command?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is a question.

flashcards.front: When is p → q false? Answer with the two values in order.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: p is true and q is false.

flashcards.front: Is p → q true or false when p is false and q is true?
flashcards.back: True: the rule is not broken.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The material conditional is true.

flashcards.front: Name the equivalent transformation of p → q.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The contrapositive is equivalent.

flashcards.front: How many assignments distinguish a conditional from its contrapositive?
flashcards.back: Zero: they agree on every assignment.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: They differ on zero assignments.

flashcards.front: How many type assignments are possible for two islanders before any claims are checked?
flashcards.back: Four assignments: each islander has two possible types.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two times two gives four assignments.

flashcards.front: A knave says “Eli is a knight.” What is Eli’s type?
flashcards.back: Eli is a knave because the statement is false.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Eli must be a knave.

flashcards.front: How many rows does a complete truth table for four independent claims need?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four independent claims require sixteen assignments.

flashcards.front: When p and q are both true, is inclusive p ∨ q true or false?
flashcards.back: True: at least one is true.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Inclusive disjunction is true.

flashcards.front: What is a claim offered as support in an argument called?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is a premise.

flashcards.front: For “p ∨ q; ¬p; therefore q”, which letter is the conclusion?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The conclusion is q.

flashcards.front: A valid argument has one false premise. Is it sound or unsound?
flashcards.back: Unsound: soundness requires every premise to be true.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The argument is unsound.

flashcards.front: How many counterexamples are compatible with validity?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Validity permits zero counterexamples.

flashcards.front: “p → q; q; therefore p” affirms which part of the conditional?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It affirms the consequent.

flashcards.front: Is “p → q; ¬q; therefore ¬p” valid or invalid?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The inference is valid.

An argument is valid when there is no case with all premises true and the conclusion false. It can still contain false premises or have a false conclusion in the actual world. Soundness adds the requirement that every premise is actually true.

Consider “p → q; q; therefore p”. Set p false and q true. Both premises hold but the conclusion fails. The argument remains invalid even if a different actual case happens to make its conclusion true. Test the guarantee, rather than one happy outcome.

A valid argument whose premises are all true is sound. A valid argument with a false premise is unsound. Truth of the conclusion alone settles neither property. First test the inference across cases, then investigate the premises with suitable evidence.

acceptedIdeas: If no log was recorded, the backup did not complete.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Reverse the direction and negate both claims: no recorded log implies no completed backup, assuming the original rule.

choices.label: If a log was recorded, the backup completed.
If no log was recorded, the backup did not complete.
If the backup did not complete, no log was recorded.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Nia: Omar is a knight.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Omar: We are the same type.

question.prompt: Knights always tell the truth and knaves always lie. Which types fit both speakers?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nia's statement requires the same type for both. Omar's statement is therefore true, so Omar is a knight and Nia is too.

choices.label: Nia is a knight; Omar is a knave
Nia is a knave; Omar is a knight

question.prompt: How many rows make (p OR q) AND NOT p true? OR is inclusive.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: NOT p excludes the two rows with p true. Of the remaining rows, p OR q is true only when q is true: one row.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The museum is closed, because today is Monday and the museum closes every Monday.

question.prompt: Which claim is this passage trying to establish?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The two claims after 'because' are offered as support for the claim that the museum is closed.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If 9 is even, 9 is divisible by 2.

statements.label: B
statements.text: 9 is even.

question.prompt: How should this argument be classified?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its form is p implies q; p; therefore q, which is valid. The premise that 9 is even is false, so the argument is unsound.

choices.label: Invalid because the conclusion is false

statements.label: A
statements.text: If the router is offline, the page fails to load.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The router is online.

question.prompt: What is the gap in this argument?

acceptedIdeas: A different fault could still prevent loading.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: This denies the antecedent. A true conditional allows an online router and a failed page; another fault can prevent loading.

choices.label: An online router guarantees every page loads.
A different fault could still prevent loading.
The first premise says the router is offline.

courseChecks.title: Bring it together
courseChecks.description: Use all eight lessons to test arguments and repair a mistaken inference. Results appear after the final response.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If a project passed the audit, it received a certificate.

statements.label: B
statements.text: This project received no certificate.

question.prompt: Assume the rule is true. A certificate was not issued. What follows?

acceptedIdeas: It did not pass the audit.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: If it had passed, it would have received a certificate. The missing certificate therefore rules out passing, but says nothing about whether an audit happened.

choices.label: It did not pass the audit.
Every uncertified project was never audited.

question.prompt: Across all four rows, how many make NOT (p AND q) true?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The conjunction is true only in the true–true row. Negating it makes each of the other three rows true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The number inside is greater than 20.

question.prompt: A sealed envelope contains a number. You have not opened it. How should you treat notice A?

acceptedIdeas: It is a claim whose truth is currently unknown to you.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The notice asserts something about a fixed number. Not knowing whether it is true does not turn it into a command or remove its classical truth value.

choices.label: It is a claim whose truth is currently unknown to you.
It has no truth value until someone opens the envelope.
It is a command to choose a larger number.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If a badge is active, the gate opens.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The gate opens.

question.prompt: Which change repairs the inference while keeping its first premise?

acceptedIdeas: Replace the second premise with 'The gate does not open' and conclude 'The badge is not active'.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With the gate closed, an active badge would contradict the first premise. That repair uses the contrapositive; the other proposed patterns do not rule out other causes.

choices.label: Keep the second premise; all effects have one cause.
Replace the second premise with 'The gate does not open' and conclude 'The badge is not active'.
Replace the second premise with 'The badge is not active' and conclude 'The gate does not open'.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Ivo: Mara is a knave.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Mara: Ivo is a knave.

question.prompt: Knights tell the truth and knaves lie. How many type assignments satisfy both statements?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Exactly one speaker must be a knight. Ivo knight with Mara knave works, and the reverse works. Both-knight and both-knave assignments contradict their statements.

statements.label: A
statements.text: p implies q.

statements.label: B
statements.text: q is true.

question.prompt: Which assignment is a counterexample to this argument?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: When p is false and q is true, both premises are true and the conclusion p is false. One such assignment refutes validity.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The sample is in cabinet 4: it is either in cabinet 4 or cabinet 9, and cabinet 9 is empty.

question.prompt: Which sentence supplies the conclusion, even though it appears first?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The alternatives and the empty cabinet support the first claim, that the sample is in cabinet 4. Position alone does not identify a premise.

choices.label: The sample is in one of the two cabinets.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If a package contains glass, it is marked G.

question.prompt: Which inspected package violates the stated implication?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The implication requires G for glass packages. It does not forbid G on other packages, so only glass without G violates it.

courseChecks.title: Use it a week later
courseChecks.description: Apply the ideas to new reports and decisions after a week. Each problem uses a fresh case.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Either valve A or valve B is leaking. Inspection ruled out A. That is why we will repair B: valve B is leaking.

question.prompt: Which claim is the conclusion of this maintenance report?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The alternatives and the inspection result are used to establish that B leaks. The proposed repair is motivated by that conclusion.

choices.label: At least one valve is leaking.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Record the room temperature.

question.prompt: Which version makes the instruction into a claim?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The last version asserts that recording occurred. It can be true or false; the alternatives remain a question and an instruction.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Premise A has been checked and is true.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Premise B has been checked and is true.

question.prompt: Both listed premises are true. What else is needed before calling the argument sound?

acceptedIdeas: There must be no case with both premises true and the conclusion false.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Soundness requires true premises and a valid inference. Validity excludes every true-premise, false-conclusion case.

choices.label: There must be no case with both premises true and the conclusion false.
The conclusion must be written after the premises.

question.prompt: A safety rule says: if the door is open, the warning lamp is on. The door is closed and the lamp is on. What does this show?

acceptedIdeas: The observation respects the rule; it does not establish what caused the light.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The rule constrains cases with an open door. A closed door with a lit lamp does not violate it or identify the cause of the light.

choices.label: The observation respects the rule; it does not establish what caused the light.
The lamp proves the door is actually open.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Lena says a forecast follows from the measurements.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A colleague objects that Lena is usually impatient.

question.prompt: Which review directly tests the reasoning?

acceptedIdeas: Check whether the measurements support the forecast.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Inspect the link between the measurements and forecast. A remark about Lena's temperament supplies no counterexample or faulty calculation.

choices.label: Count how many people dislike Lena.
Check whether the measurements support the forecast.
Reject the forecast because impatience is undesirable.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Published implies passed review.

statements.label: B
statements.text: This report did not pass review.

question.prompt: Assume every published report passed review. A report did not pass review. Which conclusion follows?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: This uses the contrapositive. Publishing would require a passed review; the rule says nothing about whether drafting happened.

choices.label: The report has never been drafted.

question.prompt: How many assignments make p AND (q OR NOT q) true? Use the four rows shown.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: q OR NOT q is true in every classical row. The whole expression is therefore true exactly in the two rows where p is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Rui: We are different types.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Sol: Rui tells the truth.

question.prompt: Each witness either always tells the truth or always lies. Which types fit these reports?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sol's report requires the same truth-telling status for both. Then Rui's claim that their types differ is false. Rui lies, and Sol's report is false too.

choices.label: Rui tells the truth; Sol lies
Rui lies; Sol tells the truth
